The test image shows a tomato stem near the soil line that has been cut longitudinally. Key features:
- White/cream material visible at the stem base (possibly mycelium)
- Stem split open showing cream-white interior pith
- Dead wilted leaves, collapsed plant
- Sandy soil, plant pulled from ground

This looks like a stem-based disease. Let me read the part index and then check reference images.
Stem/root area affected. Top candidates from stem classes: Southern_Blight, Sclerotinia_Timber_Rot, Southern_Bacterial_Wilt. Let me view reference images across 8 classes.

Now I have enough evidence to make my decision. Let me compare findings:

**Test image features:**
- Plant uprooted from sandy soil, roots visible at top
- Stem near soil line with white/gray material at exterior base
- Stem appears split/peeled showing cream-white interior
- Completely dead/collapsed plant with dry brown leaves

**Reference comparison:**
1. **Southern_Blight** (root/Bugwood_18): Uprooted plant with clear white mycelial mat at stem base, roots visible — structurally very similar to test image
2. **Southern_Blight** (stem/Bugwood_15): Stem peeled open showing cream-white interior with dark border — also matches
3. **Sclerotinia_Timber_Rot** (stem/Bugwood_4): Stem cut longitudinally with prominent black sclerotia embedded in white pith — the cutting action matches, but no visible black sclerotia in test image
4. **Southern_Bacterial_Wilt** (stem/Bugwood_13): Stem cut with brown vascular discoloration — test image shows white, not brown interior (rules this out)
5. **Alternaria** (stem): Dark black external canker near soil line — test image lacks dark concentric canker externally
6. **Phytophthora_Blight** (stem): Dark collapsing stems still in ground — different presentation

The white material at the exterior stem base near the soil line, combined with the uprooted plant composition on sandy soil, most closely matches **Southern_Blight**. No distinct black sclerotia are visible that would confirm Sclerotinia.
